uncited: - **Inputs**: A set of triangle meshes (vertices, normals), a voxel grid resolution (or step size), and an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) defining the scene bounds.
- **Outputs**: A list of occupied voxel coordinates (or a dense grid representation) and optionally per-voxel data (e.g., color, normal) stored in a buffer.
**Voxel Grid Buffer**: A 1D Shader Storage Buffer Object (SSBO) of type `int`.
-   For single-view: View and Projection matrices mapping world space to clip space, then to voxel space.
-   **Single View**: Position an orthographic camera outside the AABB along the projection axis (e.g., Z-axis).
**Allocate and Initialize Buffer**: Create an SSBO of size $\text{resolution}.x \times \text{resolution}.y \times \text{resolution}.z \times 4$ bytes.
-   **Vertex Shader**: Pass world-space positions to the next stage.
-   Compute the triangle face normal using the cross product of two edge vectors: $\vec{n} = (\vec{v_1} - \vec{v_0}) \times (\vec{v_2} - \vec{v_0})$.
-   Select the optimal camera index by comparing the absolute values of the normal components: $n_{DX} = |n_x|, n_{DY} = |n_y|, n_{DZ} = |n_z|$.
-   Receive the world-space position of the fragment ($FragPos$).
-   Compute world position: $P = min + (ix \cdot \text{step}, iy \cdot \text{step}, iz \cdot \text{step})$.
-   **Atomic Contention**: High triangle density can lead to atomic contention on the SSBO.
-   **Precision**: Floating-point precision in the fragment shader when calculating voxel indices can lead to off-by-one errors at boundaries.

An extension of single-view voxelization that uses three orthographic cameras (along X, Y, Z axes) and selects the best view for each triangle based on its normal vector to prevent cracks caused by degenerate projections.
-   **Time Complexity**: $O(N \cdot T)$, where $N$ is the number of triangles and $T$ is the average number of fragments generated per triangle.
The rasterization hardware performs the heavy lifting in parallel.
-   **Memory Complexity**: $O(V)$, where $V$ is the number of voxels in the grid ($res_x \cdot res_y \cdot res_z$).
The SSBO size grows cubically with resolution.
-   **Measured Performance**: Significantly faster than CPU-based ray-tracing methods, especially for high-resolution grids and complex meshes.
-   **Scaling**: Performance scales well with GPU parallelism but degrades if the voxel grid becomes too large for GPU memory or if atomic contention becomes severe.
